choices.label: C
choices.text: Coach the Scrum Team about the purpose of the Daily Scrum.
choices.explanation: Coaching the team on the purpose of the Daily Scrum helps them understand its true function and maintain its effectiveness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nothing. The Scrum Master does not attend the Daily Scrum.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Master should address behaviors that impact team dynamics.

questions.question:
You are the Scrum Master of a Scrum Team that is new to Scrum. The Product Owner comes to you halfway through the Sprint and says, "I do not feel like the Developers will be able to meet the forecast that they developed during Sprint Planning. 
What should you do in this situation?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add more people to the Scrum Team to meet the Product Owner's expectations.
choices.explanation: Adding more people mid-Sprint is not practical and can disrupt the team.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Agree to help the Product Owner by having a discussion with the Developers about the importance of meeting their forecast.
choices.explanation: Focusing only on meeting the forecast can add unnecessary pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Talk to the Developers. Challenge and inspire them to complete all of the work so that they meet their forecast.
choices.explanation: Challenging the team without addressing the root cause can be counterproductive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coach the Product Owner that achieving the Sprint Goal is the Scrum Team's objective. A forecast is only used to initially estimate the effort required to reach the Sprint Goal.
choices.explanation: Coaching the Product Owner to understand that achieving the Sprint Goal is the primary objective helps maintain focus and realistic expectations.

questions.question:
What is the primary concern when multiple Scrum Teams work from the same Product Backlog with the goal of creating a valuable and useful integrated Increment by the end of their Sprint?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clearly defining all requirements three Sprints ahead.
choices.explanation: Defining requirements three Sprints ahead is not flexible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maximizing velocity.
choices.explanation: Maximizing velocity does not guarantee value delivery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Making sure there is enough work for everyone on every team.
choices.explanation: Ensuring enough work for everyone is less important than delivering value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minimizing dependencies between Scrum Teams.
choices.explanation: Minimizing dependencies between Scrum Teams ensures smoother collaboration and integration of work.

questions.question:
Your Scrum Team has been working together for over a dozen Sprints. The Scrum Team consists of 10 members. Each Sprint takes four weeks. As a Scrum Master, you observe that the Developers are hardly collaborating : during the Sprint, members are primarily working on their own items. You also notice that the items on the Sprint Backlog are mostly unrelated. You suspect that the lack of a Sprint Goal might be the cause. Although you have encouraged the use of a Sprint Goal, both the Product Owner and the Developers have concluded that they are unable to create Sprint Goals based on the wide variety of items on their Product Backlog,
What might explain why this Scrum Team is struggling to craft a Sprint Goal?
(choose all that apply)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scrum Team is too big
choices.explanation: Team size alone does not explain the issue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scrum might not be the best framework for the work done by this team.
choices.explanation: If Scrum is not suitable for the team's work, it can explain the difficulty in creating a Sprint Goal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Product Owner does not have the mandate to make decisions about items on the Product Backlog nor their ordering.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner’s mandate does not directly affect Sprint Goal creation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Sprints are too long,
choices.explanation: Sprint length does not necessarily impact the ability to create a Sprint Goal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Product Owner Is not communicating the Product Goal that they want to achieve in upcoming Sprints.
choices.explanation: Without a communicated Product Goal, it’s hard to align on a Sprint Goal.

questions.question:
What is one way to determine if the Product Owner is interacting with the Developers enough throughout a Sprint?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Observe whether the Developers need to ask the Product Owner questions at times other than during the Dally Scrum.
choices.explanation: Needing to ask questions at times other than the Daily Scrum is not a definitive measure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Product Owners and Developers are satisfied with the increment.
choices.explanation: Satisfaction with the Increment indicates sufficient interaction between the Product Owner and Developers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Check the Daily Scrum reports to see whether the Product Owner was present at the majority of the Daily Scrum meetings.
choices.explanation: The Product Owner’s presence at Daily Scrums is not mandatory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Developers should determine the percentage of time the Product Owner is required to be present and monitor whether the Product Owner's average presence is around this figure.
choices.explanation: Monitoring the Product Owner’s time is not practical.

questions.question:
Which statement about the Sprint Goal is incorrect?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scrum Team commits to it.
choices.explanation: The Scrum Team commits to the Sprint Goal as a shared objective for the Sprint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Scrum Team discusses openly about alternative ways to reach it.
choices.explanation: Collaboration on how to achieve the goal is encouraged in Scrum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If it does not seem achievable, the Developers have the courage to tell the Product Owner.
choices.explanation: Courage is a Scrum value that supports open discussion when a goal seems unachievable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is only a forecast and may change within the Sprint as more is learned.
choices.explanation: The Sprint Goal should remain stable to provide focus and direction. Correct Options: A, B, C, E, and F are all correct because they accurately describe aspects of the Sprint Goal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It helps increase focus.
choices.explanation: A clear Sprint Goal helps the team stay focused during the Sprint.

choices.label: F
choices.text: The Product Owner respects the opinions of the Developers about whether they can achieve the Sprint Goal.
choices.explanation: Mutual respect ensures that the Product Owner listens to the Developers' perspective on achievability.

questions.question:
User documentation is part of your Definition of Done. However, there are not enough technical writers for all teams. Your Scrum Team does not have a technical writer. 
What needs to be done?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Your Scrum Team is still accountable for creating user documentation. In this case, the Developers will write it
choices.explanation: The Scrum Team is accountable for creating user documentation, even if it means Developers write it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Form a separate team of technical writers that will work on an on-demand basis for the various Product Owners. Work order will be first in, first out.
choices.explanation: Forming a separate team can create dependencies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Let the user documentation remain undone and accumulate until after the last development Sprint. It will then be done by any available technical writers.
choices.explanation: Leaving documentation undone is not aligned with the Definition of Done.

questions.question:
During the Sprint Review the Product Owner introduces the functionality that is likely to be done over the next Sprints. The Chief Security Officer reminds everyone that through the envisioned functionality, sensitive personal user data will be stored. This might be the subject of extemal security audits. He reminds everyone of important non-functional requirements with regards to security. These were not applicable and not considered previously.
What are two effective ways the Scrum Team can manage these high-security concerns?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are discussed, determined, and documented in parallel Sprints to not disturb the actual feature development. Once analyzed, they should be applied to the work already done before further feature development can continue.
choices.explanation: Postponing analysis can delay addressing critical security issues.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The impact of these security concerns on past and future work needs to be determined before new Sprints can start. A list of security-related Product Backlog items needs to be passed on to the Product Owner before starting the next Sprint
choices.explanation: Separating security from functional development can create coordination problems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are added to the Product Backlog and addressed throughout the next Sprints, combined with creating the business functionality in those Sprints, no matter how small that business functionality.
choices.explanation: Adding security concerns to the Product Backlog ensures they are addressed in future Sprints.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They should be managed by a separate specialist team in a parallel Sprint, so they can be specifically resolved through an improved application design without hindering functional development.
choices.explanation: Managing security in parallel can lead to integration challenges.

choices.label: E
choices.text: During the Sprint Retrospective, the Scrum Team assesses how to add these ‘expectations to the Definition of Done so every future Increment wil ive up to these requirements. If needed they can work with external specialists to better understand the requirements
choices.explanation: Assessing security concerns during the Sprint Retrospective helps integrate them into the Definition of Done.

questions.question: True or False: Using Scrum ensures that adding more resources to a project proportionally increases the value delivered.

choices.label: A
choices.text: True
choices.explanation: Adding more resources does not proportionally increase value delivered due to factors like team dynamics.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False
choices.explanation: Adding more resources does not proportionally increase value delivered due to factors like team dynamics.

questions.question:
Which four of the following risks to product development are addressed by Scrum?
(choose the best four answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The timescale of the planned work
choices.explanation: Scrum limits planning to short, timeboxed iterations to reduce timescale risk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The stability and complexity of the technology.
choices.explanation: Empirical process control helps adapt to unstable or complex technologies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The complexity and unpredictability of the requirements.
choices.explanation: Scrum addresses requirement uncertainty through iterative refinement and delivery.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The skills and working relationships of the people on the teams.
choices.explanation: Frequent collaboration and retrospectives improve team skills and relationships.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The definition of incentive and bonus strategies by Human Resources for all team members.
choices.explanation: Scrum does not address HR policies like incentives or bonuses, which are organizational concerns.

choices.label: F
choices.text: F: The clear definitions of stages and gateways in the overall governance model.
choices.explanation: Scrum replaces predefined stages with empirical control, making rigid stage-based governance irrelevant.

questions.question: True or False: When multiple Scrum Teams work on the same product, they should employ a "Definition of Ready" to maximize their velocity. A "Definition of Ready" ensures that Sprint Planning can end within its timebox. This has a positive effect on the team's velocity, as the team will have more time for productive work.

choices.label: A
choices.text: True
choices.explanation: The "Definition of Ready" is not a requirement in Scrum. It’s a popular practice in some teams, but not part of the Scrum Guide. Also, it does not guarantee higher velocity or better timeboxing in Sprint Planning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False
choices.explanation: The "Definition of Ready" is not a requirement in Scrum. It’s a popular practice in some teams, but not part of the Scrum Guide. Also, it does not guarantee higher velocity or better timeboxing in Sprint Planning.

questions.question:
Scrum Teams using Kanban can start to increase predictability by:
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Improving transparency by having a CFD, Control Chart and Aging chart.
choices.explanation: These charts increase transparency but do not by themselves make flow more predictable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inspecting and adapting the Product Backlog during the Sprint Review.
choices.explanation: Backlog refinement affects what is worked on, not how predictable the flow is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reducing the amount of work in progress by introducing Work in Progress (WIP) Limits.
choices.explanation: Limiting WIP stabilizes the system and reduces variability, directly improving predictability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Visualizing the Workflow using a Kanban board.
choices.explanation: Visualization helps inspection but does not improve predictability without WIP limits.

questions.question:
What are the two things that constitute a Kanban board?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Visualization of your Workflow.
choices.explanation: Visualization makes the flow of work transparent and enables inspection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Class of service.
choices.explanation: Classes of service are optional policies, not required parts of a Kanban board.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Work in Progress (WIP) Limits.
choices.explanation: WIP limits turn the workflow into a pull system, which is essential for Kanban.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Swim lanes per Product Backlog item type.
choices.explanation: Swimlanes are visualization tools but not required by the Kanban Guide.

questions.question:
Which of the following is NOT an essential component to initially achieving flow?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inspecting & adapting your Workflow.
choices.explanation: Inspection and adaptation are key to establishing and maintaining flow.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Actively managing WIP.
choices.explanation: Managing WIP is central to stabilizing and improving flow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ensuring the Product Backlog is refined frequently.
choices.explanation: Backlog refinement affects planning, not the establishment of flow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Visualizing your Workflow.
choices.explanation: Visualization is one of the two foundations of Kanban.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Limiting Work in Progress (WIP).
choices.explanation: WIP limits are essential for creating flow and reducing bottlenecks.

questions.question:
Which of these is NOT a good description of Cycle Time?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The time a work item takes from initial idea/concept to feedback returned from customers after a production release.
choices.explanation: This describes Lead Time, which is related but still a valid time measurement; it’s not incorrect enough to be the 'NOT good' choice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The time a work item starts until when it finishes.
choices.explanation: This is the proper definition of Cycle Time and therefore a good description.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The length of time a work item stays in one column.
choices.explanation: This measures part of the Cycle Time, which is useful for analyzing bottlenecks, so it’s still a good description.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The number of items that move into the delivery/end point per time period (e.g., daily/weekly).
choices.explanation: This defines Throughput, not Cycle Time — it measures quantity, not duration.

questions.question:
When the Developers limit Work in Progress (WIP) inside a Sprint, what would you expect to observe?
(choose the best three answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The amount of work done by the end of the Sprint would be reduced.
choices.explanation: Limiting WIP usually increases finished work by reducing multitasking.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Self-management would be strengthened as a result of increased transparency.
choices.explanation: WIP limits create transparency that supports self-organization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased collaboration/swarming between the Developers.
choices.explanation: Fewer concurrent items encourage developers to swarm and finish together.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Developers would stop beginning work, and instead, start finishing work.
choices.explanation: Limiting WIP shifts focus from starting new work to finishing current work.

questions.question:
How does Kanban for Scrum Teams maximize value delivered?
(choose the best two answers)

choices.label: A
choices.text: By optimizing the flow of value.
choices.explanation: This answer aligns with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams principles and demonstrates correct application of Kanban within the Scrum framework.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By minimizing transaction costs.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By choosing higher-value items to deliver.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By minimizing time spent in meetings/events.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: E
choices.text: By enabling tighter empirical feedback loops via faster Cycle Times.
choices.explanation: This answer aligns with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams principles and demonstrates correct application of Kanban within the Scrum framework.

questions.question:
In which of these situations should the Scrum Team adjust their Work in Progress (WIP) Limits?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: When they see that the average story size they are working on is growing.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When they have extra capacity during the Sprint and want to start some new work items from the Sprint Backlog.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When they want to improve their Cycle Time, flow, and focus.
choices.explanation: This answer aligns with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams principles and demonstrates correct application of Kanban within the Scrum framework.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When there is unplanned urgent work that emerges during the Sprint.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

questions.question:
Which metric makes most sense to look at during Sprint Planning?
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Service Level Expectation.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Work in Progress.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Throughput.
choices.explanation: This answer aligns with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams principles and demonstrates correct application of Kanban within the Scrum framework.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Work Item Aging.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

questions.question:
Little's Law states that:
(choose the best answer)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Average Cycle Time = Average Work in Progress / Average Throughput.
choices.explanation: This answer aligns with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams principles and demonstrates correct application of Kanban within the Scrum framework.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Average Throughput = Average Cycle Time * Average Work in Progress.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Average Work in Progress = Average Cycle Time / Average Throughput.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Average Throughput = Average Cycle Time / Average Work in Progress.
choices.explanation: This answer does not align with the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams or does not represent an effective Kanban practice in a Scrum context.

questions.question:
When is the most appropriate time for Scrum Teams practicing professional Scrum with Kanban to inspect and adapt their Work in Progress (WIP) Limits?
(choose the best answer)
